blocks.prompt: The First Ones to Fly Were Farm Animals
blocks.text: A long time ago, two brothers in France made a giant balloon out of cloth and paper. They lit a fire under it. The hot air went inside. The balloon got fat and lifted off the ground. Nobody knew if the sky was safe to breathe. So the brothers sent up three animals first. A sheep, a duck, and a rooster rode in the basket. A king and queen watched them go. The balloon flew for eight minutes. It came down in the trees. The sheep was fine. The duck was fine. The rooster was fine too. After that, people were brave enough to fly.

blocks.prompt: Hot Air Wants to Go Up
blocks.text: Blow up a balloon and let it go. It falls to the floor. So how does a balloon big enough to hold people climb into the sky? The answer is heat. Air is made of tiny bits called molecules, all bouncing around. When you heat air, the bits bounce harder and spread further apart. A bucket of warm air holds fewer bits than the same bucket of cold air, so it weighs less. The heavier cold air around it sinks and shoves the warm air up. That is why smoke rises from a fire. A hot air balloon uses that trick on purpose. The huge cloth bag, called the envelope, has a hole in the bottom. A burner sits under the hole and shoots a flame of burning propane straight up inside. The air in the envelope gets to about 100 degrees Celsius, as hot as boiling water. The cool air outside slides underneath and lifts the whole thing: bag, basket, pilot, and all. To go down, the pilot pulls a rope. A flap at the very top opens and hot air spills out. Cool air moves in. The balloon sinks, gently.

answers: they bounce harder and spread further apart
the envelope
about 100 degrees Celsius, as hot as boiling water
(inference: the burner flame has to reach the air inside to heat it)

blocks.prompt: Wrong About Everything Except the Flying
blocks.text: In the summer of 1783, two French brothers, Joseph and Etienne Montgolfier, filled a paper and cloth bag with smoke from a fire and watched it climb over their town. They had made the first hot air balloon. They were also completely wrong about why it worked. They believed the smoke itself carried a special lifting power, which they named Montgolfier gas, and they fed the fire damp straw and wool to make the smoke thick. The smoke did nothing. Heat was doing all the work. Word reached the king. Louis the Sixteenth wanted a demonstration, and he wanted to know whether the air high above the ground was safe to breathe. Nobody had ever been up there to find out. The king suggested testing it on prisoners. The brothers proposed a different crew. On the nineteenth of September 1783, a balloon lifted off from the palace at Versailles carrying a sheep, a duck, and a rooster. The choices were deliberate. The sheep stood in for a person, because its body works much like ours. The duck already flew, so it was the check: if the duck came down sick, the balloon itself was to blame. The rooster was a bird that stays low, one more way to compare. The balloon rose, drifted about two miles, and came down in the woods after eight minutes. All three animals walked away unharmed. Two months later, two men climbed into a basket over Paris and stayed up for twenty five minutes. Human flight had begun, and a sheep had gone first.

notes: No rudder, no propeller, no steering wheel

The Albuquerque Box: south low, north high

blocks.prompt: The Vehicle With No Steering Wheel
blocks.text: A hot air balloon has no rudder, no propeller, and no steering wheel. There is nothing to turn. A balloon does not travel through the air; it becomes part of the air, and it goes exactly where the air goes. Ask a balloon pilot how they steer and you will get an honest answer: they do not. What they do is choose. The atmosphere is not one moving thing. It is stacked in layers, and those layers rarely agree. Near the ground, friction drags at the wind and bends its direction. A few hundred feet up, the wind may be blowing twenty degrees to the right of the surface wind. A thousand feet higher, it may be heading somewhere else again. The pilot has only one control that matters: up and down. Burn to climb, vent to sink, and each new altitude hands the balloon a different wind. Steering a balloon means reading the stack and moving between floors. Pilots learn the stack before they leave the ground. They release a small helium balloon, called a pibal, and watch which way it drifts as it rises. Some places have layers so reliable that they have names. At Albuquerque, in New Mexico, cold air sliding down the river valley pushes balloons south near the ground while the wind higher up carries them north, so a careful pilot can fly out, climb, ride back, and land near the launch field. Balloonists call it the Box. The choosing has limits. If every layer is heading east, the balloon heads east. A pilot cannot stop, cannot hover in place against a breeze, and cannot pick a landing field the way an airplane picks a runway. They can only aim, and a chase crew drives the roads below, watching the sky, ready to collect the balloon wherever the air decides to put it down. This is also why balloons fly at dawn. Early morning air is calm and layered and predictable. By midday the sun has heated the ground, the air churns upward in thermals, the layers blur together, and the one thing a balloon pilot depends on is gone.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Archimedes: lift equals the weight of the air pushed aside
Air at 100C is about a fifth lighter than at 20C
A 2,800 cubic meter envelope lifts roughly 700 kg
Envelope: thin nylon, with Nomex near the flame
Basket: still woven wicker, for the landing shock
Altitude record: 21,027 meters, set in 2005

blocks.prompt: Nothing Holds It Up But a Difference
blocks.text: A hot air balloon is the simplest flying machine ever built, and understanding it requires giving up one comfortable idea: that flight is about pushing air out of the way. An airplane fights the sky. It burns fuel to force itself forward, and the wing turns that forward motion into lift. A balloon fights nothing. It sits in the air the way a cork sits in water, and it rises for exactly the reason the cork rises, which Archimedes worked out more than two thousand years before anyone thought to fly. The rule is this: any object in a fluid is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. Air is a fluid. An envelope holding 2,800 cubic meters of air displaces 2,800 cubic meters of atmosphere, and the atmosphere pushes back with a force equal to what that volume of outside air weighs. If the air inside weighs less than the air shoved aside, the balloon climbs. Nothing holds it up but a difference. The burner creates that difference, and it does so by removing air, which sounds backward. The mouth of the envelope is open at the bottom and never closes. Heat the air inside and it expands, and since the bag cannot stretch, the surplus spills out of the open mouth. What is left is the same volume of air holding fewer molecules, and therefore weighing less. At 100 degrees Celsius, air is about a fifth lighter than air at 20 degrees. A fifth of very little is still not much. That 2,800 cubic meter envelope produces around 700 kilograms of lift, and that must carry the fabric, the burner, the propane, the basket, and the people. This is why balloons are enormous, and why they cannot be made small. A balloon built to carry only you would still need to be the size of a house. The physics dictates everything else about the machine. The envelope is thin nylon, because every gram of fabric is borrowed from the payload, with fire-resistant Nomex sewn in around the mouth where the flame is. The basket is still woven wicker, a material older than writing, because nothing modern beats it: it is light, it flexes, and it soaks up the shock of a landing the pilot cannot fully control. The pilot cannot fully control it because a balloon has no steering. It travels with the wind, at the speed of the wind, which is why the flame is loud and the ride is silent. There is no wind in a balloon basket. You are the wind. The Montgolfier brothers built the first one in 1783 without understanding any of this. They thought the smoke was the lifting agent and fed their fire wool and damp straw to thicken it. The smoke was irrelevant. The heat was everything. They were wrong about the mechanism and right about the machine, which happens more often in the history of invention than anyone admits. Two centuries of refinement have changed the balloon less than you would expect. Propane replaced straw. Nylon replaced taffeta. In 2005, Vijaypat Singhania rode a hot air balloon to 21,027 meters over Mumbai, nearly twice the cruising altitude of an airliner, breathing bottled oxygen, because at that height the air is too thin to breathe and too thin to push back with much force. But the machine that carried him was the Montgolfiers' machine: a bag, a fire, and a difference in weight between the inside and the outside.
